worksheets.title: Distance, time and speed (core)
worksheets.context: This sheet checks that you can work out and compare speeds, and that you know what an average and a reference point are.

items.p: Meera runs 100 metres in 20 seconds. Lakshmi runs 60 metres in 10 seconds. Who is faster?
items.why: Meera covers 5 metres in each second. Lakshmi covers 6. Choosing Meera compares only the distances and forgets the times.

items.p: A bus goes 120 kilometres in 3 hours. Its speed is ____ kilometres per hour.
items.why: 120 ÷ 3 = 40. The bus covers 40 kilometres in each hour.

items.p: A car that covers 10 metres in its first second must cover 20 metres in two seconds.
items.why: False. That is true only if the speed never changes. A car that is speeding up covers more, and a car that is slowing down covers less.

items.p: A scooter covers 20 kilometres in one hour, with stops at signals. Its needle showed 40 for a while. What was its average speed?
items.why: Average speed is the whole distance divided by the whole time, so 20 ÷ 1 = 20. The 40 was the speed at one moment, not the average.

items.p: Sort each one by what it tells you.
items: the number on a scooter's speedometer right now
Speed at one moment
a train's 400 kilometres divided by its 5 hours
Average speed
a cricket ball's speed just as it leaves the bowler's hand
Speed at one moment
a girl's 3 kilometres to school divided by her 36 minutes
Average speed
the speed shown on a bus's display as it passes a toll gate
Speed at one moment
items.why: An average uses a whole trip, with its fast parts, slow parts and stops. A single reading uses a tiny piece of the trip.

items.p: Match each speed to the mover it suits best.
pairs: a bus on a main road
items.why: Each pair fits the size of the distance and the time. A continent needs a whole year to move a few centimetres, and a bus needs only an hour to cover many kilometres.

items.p: Put these movers in order from slowest to fastest.
a: A train on a main line
items.why: A snail covers about a millimetre each second. A walking child covers about 1 metre or more each second. A bicycle and a train cover more again.

items.p: Rohan says, 'Ria ran 50 metres and I ran 40 metres, so Ria is faster.' What is missing from what he says?
items.a: The time each of them took. Faster means more distance in the same time, so 50 metres in 20 seconds could be slower than 40 metres in 10 seconds.
items.why: A strong answer asks for both measurements and gives an example where the longer distance is the slower run.

items.p: Why do you think the second metre of a rolling toy car often takes longer than the first? Give your idea and say how you could test it.
items.a: Answers vary. A good idea is that the floor and the air rub against the car and slow it down. A test is to time two pieces of the track and compare the speeds, or to roll the car on a rougher floor and see if the slowing grows.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason and a way to check it, and does not say the car 'just gets tired'.

items.p: Draw the track for a toy car test. Mark where the car starts, where the stopwatch starts and stops, and the distance between the lines.
items.a: A start line, a finish line a measured distance apart such as 200 centimetres, an arrow for the car's path, and the words 'start the clock' at the start line and 'stop the clock' at the finish line.
items.why: A speed needs a measured distance and a time for exactly that distance, so the clock must start and stop at the lines.

items.p: Two ways to decide who is faster.

views.says: Give everyone the same distance. The one who takes the least time is the fastest.

views.who: A player of a hopping game (an imagined view)
views.says: Give everyone the same time. The one who goes the farthest is the fastest.

items.ask: Which would you use for 'who can hop the farthest in one minute'? Could either one be unfair?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says each way gives the same order when speeds stay steady, so neither is wrong. The same-time way suits a hopping game because nobody has to wait for the slowest finisher.
items.why: Both are fair ways to compare. One keeps distance the same and compares times. The other keeps time the same and compares distances.

items.p: A passenger asleep in a moving bus has a speed of zero.
items.why: False unless we say what the speed is compared with. Compared with the seat it is zero. Compared with the road it is the bus's speed.

items.p: Gita and Anu hop for 10 seconds with steps of the same size. Gita makes 9 hops and Anu makes 12. Who is faster?
items.why: The time is the same, so the one who went farther is faster. Anu covered 12 hop-lengths and Gita covered 9.

items.p: A snail covers 3 centimetres in 10 seconds. In one minute, at the same speed, the snail covers ____ centimetres.
items.why: One minute is 6 lots of 10 seconds, and 6 × 3 = 18 centimetres.

items.p: A toy car covers 2 metres in 4 seconds. How many centimetres does it cover in each second?
items.why: 2 metres is 200 centimetres, and 200 ÷ 4 = 50 centimetres per second.

items.p: Which of these is a complete way to state a speed?
items.why: A speed needs a distance and a time together. '40' and '40 kilometres' leave out the time.

worksheets.title: Averages, graphs and different watchers (stretch)
worksheets.context: This sheet asks you to use speeds in harder situations, such as trips with changing speed, moving trains and very fast or very slow movers.

items.p: A girl runs the first 5 kilometres of a 10 kilometres run at 10 kilometres per hour and the last 5 kilometres at 15 kilometres per hour. What is her average speed?
items.why: The first half takes 30 minutes and the second half takes 20 minutes, so 10 kilometres takes 50 minutes. 10 kilometres in 50 minutes is 12 kilometres per hour. Adding 10 and 15 and halving it forgets that she spent longer going slowly.

items.p: A car goes at 72 kilometres per hour. In metres per second, that is ____.
items.why: 72 kilometres is 72,000 metres and one hour is 3,600 seconds. 72,000 ÷ 3,600 = 20.

items.p: Two trains on parallel tracks both go 80 kilometres per hour in the same direction. A passenger in one sees the other going 80 kilometres per hour.
items.why: False. Compared with the passenger, the other train is not moving, because both go along together. The 80 is its speed compared with the ground.

items.p: A bus goes 40 kilometres per hour. A passenger walks towards the back at 4 kilometres per hour. Compared with the road, her speed is
items.why: Her walking takes away from the bus's speed, since she goes the opposite way. 40 - 4 = 36. Adding is for walking towards the front.

items.p: Put these in order from slowest to fastest.
items.why: A continent moves a few centimetres in a year. A snail moves about a millimetre in a second. Sound moves about 340 metres in a second. A spacecraft in orbit moves several kilometres in a second. Light moves about 3 lakh kilometres in a second.

items.p: Match each speed of the same sleeping bus passenger to what it is compared with.
pairs: more than one lakh kilometres per hour
items.why: One passenger has three correct speeds because each one answers a different 'compared with what'.

items.p: Sort each mover by how its speed behaves.
items: the tip of a clock's second hand
Steady speed
a toy car rolling to a stop
Changing speed
a ceiling fan just after it is switched on
Changing speed
a ceiling fan on one setting for an hour
Steady speed
an autorickshaw in a market lane
Changing speed
items.why: A steady speed means equal distances take equal times. A mover that starts, stops, speeds up or slows down does not keep one speed.

items.p: A boat's rower pulls at 5 kilometres per hour in still water. The river flows at 3 kilometres per hour. Explain why her speed is different compared with the bank and compared with the water.
items.a: Compared with the water she goes 5. Compared with the bank it depends on the direction. Going with the river she goes 8, and against it she goes 2. The water itself moves compared with the bank.
items.why: A strong answer names both reference points and shows the adding or taking away for each direction.

items.p: How could two friends measure the speed of sound across a field with a stopwatch and a clapper made of two flat sticks? Say what they would measure and what could go wrong.
items.a: One friend stands a measured distance away, such as 200 metres, and claps the sticks. The other starts the stopwatch when she sees the clap and stops it when she hears it. Speed is distance divided by time. The time is only about half a second, so a late finger spoils it. They should repeat it many times and use the middle value, or use a longer distance.
items.why: A strong answer includes a measured distance, a time, the sum, and the problem that light arrives almost at once while the finger is slow.

items.p: Draw a graph with time across and distance up for a bus that moves steadily, stops for 10 minutes at a dhaba, then moves steadily again.
items.a: A sloping straight line, then a flat line for the stop, then another sloping line. The two sloping parts can have different steepness.
items.why: On a distance and time graph, steepness shows speed. A flat line means the distance is not changing, so the speed is zero.

items.p: A driver and a police officer look at the same journey.

views.who: A driver planning a journey (an imagined view)
views.says: The average speed matters most. It tells me when I will arrive.

views.who: A traffic police officer (an imagined view)
views.says: The speed at each moment matters most. A fast moment near a school can hurt someone, whatever the average is.

items.ask: Which would you ask for first? Does either one make the other useless?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says each one answers a different question. The average answers 'when will I get there' and the moment answers 'how risky is this place now'. Neither makes the other useless.
items.why: An average hides the fast and slow parts of a trip, and a single reading hides the rest of the trip. Which one is the right one depends on the question.

items.p: Car A covers 30 metres in 5 seconds. Car B covers 42 metres in 7 seconds. What is true?
opts: Car A is faster, it took less time
Car B is faster, it went farther
They go at the same speed
items.why: Both go 6 metres in each second. Looking only at the time or only at the distance gives a wrong answer.

items.p: A cyclist goes 18 kilometres in 90 minutes. How many kilometres per hour is that?
items.why: 90 minutes is 1.5 hours, and 18 ÷ 1.5 = 12 kilometres per hour.

items.p: If you run fast enough beside a beam of light, you can catch up with it.
items.why: False. Everyone who measures a beam of light finds the same speed, however fast they themselves are moving. This is different from the bus and the walking passenger, and nobody has found a way round it.

items.p: A continent drifts 5 centimetres each year. In 2 crore years it moves ____ kilometres.
items.why: 2 crore is 20,000,000. 5 × 20,000,000 = 100,000,000 centimetres, which is 1,000 kilometres.

items.p: A radio signal, which travels at the speed of light, takes 20 minutes to reach Earth from a spacecraft. About how far away is the spacecraft?
items.why: 20 minutes is 1,200 seconds. Light covers 3 lakh kilometres in each second, so 3 lakh × 1,200 = 36 crore kilometres.

worksheets.title: Faulty sums and open questions (challenge)
worksheets.context: This sheet gives you tricky sums, questions about how to test an idea, and some questions with more than one good answer.

items.p: A bus covers 60 kilometres at 30 kilometres per hour and then 60 kilometres at 60 kilometres per hour. A friend says its average speed is 45. What is right?
items.why: The first 60 kilometres takes 2 hours and the second takes 1 hour. 120 ÷ 3 = 40. The bus spent longer going slowly, so the average is closer to 30 than to 60.

items.p: You can find a car's exact speed at one instant by dividing the distance by the time for that instant.
items.why: False. At one instant no time has passed and no distance is covered, so the sum has nothing to work with. We get close by timing shorter and shorter pieces, and the answer settles towards one number.

items.p: A toy car takes 1.5 seconds for the first metre and 2.5 seconds for the second metre. Its average speed over both metres is ____ centimetres per second.
items.why: 200 centimetres in 4 seconds is 50 centimetres per second.

items.p: A boat goes 12 kilometres per hour in still water. The river flows at 4 kilometres per hour. How fast does the boat go down the river, compared with the bank?
items.why: Going with the flow, the two speeds add, so 12 + 4 = 16. Going up the river would give 12 - 4 = 8.

items.p: A friend says slow things do not matter. Give two slow movers, one from the ground and one from a living being, and say why their slowness matters.
items.a: Answers vary. A drifting continent builds mountains such as the Himalayas over millions of years because it moves steadily. A root or a sprout grows a few millimetres each day, and their slowness lets them keep adjusting to light, water and soil.
items.why: A strong answer names the mover, says how slow it is, and says what its slowness makes possible.

items.p: Put these in order of the time each takes to cover 1 kilometre, from least time to most time.
a: An autorickshaw at 30 kilometres per hour
A bicycle at 15 kilometres per hour
A runner at 10 kilometres per hour
A walker at 5 kilometres per hour
items.why: They take 2, 4, 6 and 12 minutes. The faster the mover, the less time each kilometre needs.

items.p: Match each speed with the same speed in other words.
items.why: One metre per second is 3.6 kilometres per hour, because 1,000 metres make a kilometre and 3,600 seconds make an hour.

items.p: You see a firework flash and hear the bang 9 seconds later. The firework is 3 kilometres away. About how fast did the sound travel?
items.why: 3,000 metres ÷ 9 seconds is about 333 metres per second. The light arrived almost at once, so the 9 seconds belong to the sound.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Kilometres per hour, centimetres per year, litres per minute, metres per second.
items.a: Litres per minute, because it measures how much water or air flows and not how far something moves. The other three are distance in some time.
items.why: A speed always has a distance on top and a time below. Litres measure an amount, not a distance.

items.p: A cheetah can sprint at about 100 kilometres per hour. A tiny beetle moves far slower. Who is faster?

views.who: A coach counting top speed (an imagined view)
views.says: Count kilometres per hour. The cheetah is far faster.

views.who: A biologist counting body lengths (an imagined view)
views.says: Count body lengths covered each second. Many small animals beat the cheetah, because their bodies are so short.

views.who: A hungry animal's view (an imagined view)
views.says: Only the speed that catches food or escapes danger matters. A beetle needs far less ground than a cheetah does.

items.ask: Which way of comparing would you pick, and what does it leave out?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says each way answers a different question and no one way is the only fair one. Top speed ignores size, body lengths ignore how far an animal needs to go, and the third ignores that a comparison is wanted.
items.why: Which animal is 'faster' depends on what you count. All three ways are real, and scientists use each one for different questions.

items.p: Predict how a steeper ramp changes the time a toy car takes over 2 metres of floor. Say how you would test your idea fairly.
items.a: A steeper ramp lets the car start the floor with more speed, so the time should be shorter. A fair test changes only the ramp height, keeps the same car, floor and release point, and repeats each run about five times and uses the middle value.
items.why: A strong answer gives a guess with a reason and keeps everything but the ramp the same.

items.p: Draw a distance and time graph for a car that keeps speeding up. Say how the steepness of the line shows this.
items.a: A line that starts flat and curves upwards, getting steeper. The steeper the line, the more distance in each second, so the speed grows.
items.why: The steepness of a distance and time graph is the speed. A line that bends steeper means the speed is growing.

items.p: The Moon is about 3.8 lakh kilometres away. Light covers 3 lakh kilometres in each second. About how many seconds does moonlight take to reach us? Give one decimal place.
items.why: 380,000 ÷ 300,000 is about 1.3 seconds. When you look at the Moon, you see it as it was just over a second ago.

items.p: A train going 100 kilometres per hour passes another going 60 kilometres per hour on the next track, in the opposite direction. How fast does one train's passenger see the other going?
items.why: Going towards each other, the speeds add, so 100 + 60 = 160. The 40 would be right for trains going the same way.

items.p: A snail at 1 millimetre per second moves more than 100,000 times faster than a continent drifting at 5 centimetres each year.
items.why: True. A year has about 31 million seconds, so a snail covers about 31 million millimetres, which is 3 million centimetres. 3 million ÷ 5 is about 600,000 times.

items.p: Write one question about speed that nobody can answer yet. Say how someone might begin to find out.
items.a: Answers vary. A good one is 'Why does the universe have a top speed?' A way to begin is to test, with better and better experiments, whether anything carrying a message ever goes faster than light, and to look for reasons in the theories that predict the limit.
items.why: A strong answer is a real open question and suggests a test or an observation, not a guess dressed as a fact.

quiz.p: Car A covers 3 metres in 2 seconds. Car B covers 5 metres in 4 seconds. Which is faster?
opts: Car B, because it went farther
quiz.why: Car A covers 1.5 metres in each second and Car B covers 1.25. If you chose Car B, you compared only the distances. Divide each distance by its time before you compare.

quiz.p: A cyclist rides 30 kilometres and a walker walks 6 kilometres. Is the cyclist surely faster?
opts: No, we need each time too
quiz.why: Speed needs distance and time together. If the walker took 1 hour and the cyclist took 10, the walker was faster. If you chose yes, ask for both numbers first.

quiz.p: A toy car covers 150 centimetres in 3 seconds. Which working finds its speed?
quiz.why: Speed is distance divided by time. 3 ÷ 150 gives seconds for each centimetre, which is the upside-down question. Multiplying gives nothing useful.

quiz.p: You want to test if a heavier toy car rolls faster down a ramp. Which test is fair?
opts: Use a steeper ramp for the heavy car
Same ramp, add weight, repeat the run
Run each car once and compare
quiz.why: A fair test changes only one thing, here the weight, and repeats the run. A steeper ramp changes two things. A single run can be spoiled by a late finger on the stopwatch.

quiz.p: You time a car five times and get 3.1, 3.0, 3.4, 3.1 and 3.2 seconds. Why use the middle value?
opts: One run is as good as five
A late or early finger spoils some runs
The car speeds up on every run
quiz.why: A finger on a stopwatch is never exactly on time, so single runs are a little off. The middle value is not pulled away by one odd run.

quiz.p: A bus covers 120 kilometres in 3 hours. Its speedometer never showed exactly 40. Is that possible?
opts: No, the average must appear on the speedometer
Yes, it was faster and slower than 40 at times
quiz.why: The average is the whole distance divided by the whole time. A bus can be faster than 40 for some of the trip and slower for the rest, so the needle may never rest on 40.

quiz.p: Why does timing a very short piece of track give a better speed at one moment?
opts: The speed has little time to change inside it
A stopwatch works better on short times
quiz.why: Over a short piece, the speed hardly changes, so the average over that piece is close to the speed at that moment. A stopwatch is actually worse on very short times.

quiz.p: On a graph with time across and distance up, a line rises steadily, goes flat, then rises more steeply. What happened?
quiz.why: The steepness shows the speed. Flat means the distance did not change, so the mover stopped. A steeper line afterwards means a higher speed.

quiz.p: A girl sleeps in a moving train. Which is true?
opts: Zero compared with the seat, large compared with the ground
She has no speed while asleep
quiz.why: A speed always needs 'compared with what'. She is still compared with the seat, and she is moving compared with the ground. Being asleep changes nothing about the numbers.

quiz.p: A cyclist rides beside a bus and keeps exactly the same speed. Compared with the bus, her speed is
opts: The same as the bus's speed
quiz.why: Compared with the bus, she does not get nearer or farther, so her speed is zero. The bus's speed is her speed compared with the road, and that is a different question.

quiz.p: A snail, a spacecraft and a drifting continent all have speeds. Why can we compare them?
opts: Each speed is distance divided by time
Only things we can see have real speeds
Speed means something different for each
quiz.why: The sum is the same for all of them. Only the size of the distance and the time changes, which is why we use millimetres per second for one and kilometres per second for another.

quiz.p: How could anyone show that a continent moves 5 centimetres each year?
opts: Measure one spot for years with satellites
Measure it once with a long tape
quiz.why: A speed that small needs a long time to build up a distance we can measure. A film of one hour would show nothing, and one measurement gives no change to divide by a time.

quiz.p: A spaceship moving at half the speed of light shines a torch forwards. Someone at rest measures the beam. What do they find?
opts: One and a half times light's speed
quiz.why: Everyone who measures light in empty space finds the same speed. That is different from a passenger walking in a bus, where speeds add. Scientists tested this many times and it holds.

quiz.p: Which question about speed has no agreed answer yet?
opts: How fast sound travels in air
Why the universe has a top speed at all
How far a car goes in an hour at 30 kilometres per hour
quiz.why: The other two can be measured or worked out with a sum. Nobody has an agreed reason why light's speed is the limit, so the question is still open.

maths.problem: In the toy car test, a car takes 2 seconds for the first metre and 3 seconds for the second metre. Find its speed in centimetres per second for each metre and for the whole 2 metres. Then say why the whole-track speed is not exactly in the middle of the other two.
maths.answer: First metre 50, second metre about 33, whole track 40 centimetres per second. The middle of 50 and 33 is about 42, but the car spent longer going slowly.
maths.explain: First metre: 100 ÷ 2 = 50. Second metre: 100 ÷ 3 = 33.3. Whole track: 200 ÷ 5 = 40. The car spent 3 seconds at the slower speed and only 2 seconds at the faster, so the average is pulled towards the slower speed.
maths.context: This problem uses the numbers from a two-metre toy car run to compare the speed of each metre with the average.
maths.why_maths: Average speed is the whole distance over the whole time, not the middle of two speeds. This is the sum that scientists and drivers really use.

maths.problem: A child walks at 1.5 metres per second. What is that in kilometres per hour? Show how the numbers 1,000 and 3,600 come in.
maths.explain: In one hour she walks 1.5 × 3,600 = 5,400 metres. 5,400 metres is 5.4 kilometres. The 3,600 is the seconds in an hour and the 1,000 is the metres in a kilometre. So one metre per second is 3.6 kilometres per hour.
maths.context: This problem changes a walking speed from the units of the stopwatch test to the units of road signs.
maths.why_maths: Speeds are written in different units on a stopwatch and on a road sign. Changing between them keeps the same speed and changes only the measuring.

maths.problem: A bus makes a trip of 180 kilometres in 4 hours, including a 30 minute tea stop. Find its average speed for the whole trip, and its speed while it was moving. Why are they different?
maths.answer: Average 45 kilometres per hour. Moving speed about 51 kilometres per hour.
maths.explain: Whole trip: 180 ÷ 4 = 45. Moving time is 4 hours minus half an hour, which is 3.5 hours. 180 ÷ 3.5 is about 51.4. The stop adds time but no distance, so it pulls the average down.
maths.context: This problem separates the speed of a bus on the road from its average speed over a whole journey with a stop.
maths.why_maths: Time spent standing still still counts in an average speed. This is why a trip's average is always lower than the speed while moving.

maths.problem: A girl rides a bicycle and notes her distance every 10 minutes. After 10 minutes: 5 kilometres. After 20 minutes: 10 kilometres. After 30 minutes: 10 kilometres. After 40 minutes: 18 kilometres. Find her speed in kilometres per hour in each 10 or 20 minute stretch. Which stretch would be the steepest on a graph?
maths.answer: First 20 minutes: 30 kilometres per hour. Next 10 minutes: 0. Last 10 minutes: 48 kilometres per hour. The last stretch is the steepest.
maths.explain: First 20 minutes: 10 kilometres in a third of an hour is 30 kilometres per hour. Next 10 minutes: the distance did not change, so 0. Last 10 minutes: 8 kilometres in one sixth of an hour is 48 kilometres per hour. The steepest line is the one with the highest speed.
maths.context: This problem reads a table of distance and time, the same table you would use to draw a graph of a toy car or a bicycle.
maths.why_maths: The steepness of a distance and time graph is the speed. Reading steepness from numbers is how scientists find speed from data.

maths.problem: India is about 3,200 kilometres long from north to south. How long would light take to cross it, at 3 lakh kilometres per second? How long would a bus at 50 kilometres per hour take? How many times longer is the bus's time?
maths.answer: Light about one hundredth of a second. The bus 64 hours. The bus takes about 22 crore times as long.
maths.explain: Light: 3,200 ÷ 300,000 is about 0.0107 seconds. Bus: 3,200 ÷ 50 = 64 hours, which is 64 × 3,600 = 230,400 seconds. 230,400 ÷ 0.0107 is about 21.6 crore. A whole country is a tiny trip for light.
maths.context: This problem uses the speed of light to compare very different journeys across the same country.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one time by another tells you how many times faster something is. Scientists use these ratios to feel the size of very large numbers.

maths.problem: A toy car is 10 centimetres long and goes 50 centimetres per second. A bus is 10 metres long and goes 10 metres per second. Which one covers more of its own length each second? How many times more?
maths.answer: The toy car. It covers 5 of its own lengths each second. The bus covers 1. So the toy car covers 5 times as many.
maths.explain: Toy car: 50 ÷ 10 = 5 lengths each second. Bus: 10 ÷ 10 = 1 length each second. 5 ÷ 1 = 5. The bus is the faster mover in metres per second, and the toy car is faster in lengths per second.
maths.context: This problem compares two movers by a second measure, their own length, the way a biologist compares a small animal with a big one.
maths.why_maths: The answer to 'who is faster' depends on what is counted. Scaling the speed by size is a real way scientists compare animals of very different sizes.

jokes.j: What did the snail say while riding on the tortoise's back?
What did the speedometer say to the scooter?
jokes.a: 'Do not worry, I will not tell anyone you were going so fast.' (Then it told everyone.)

jokes.j: Why does lightning always win the race against thunder?
jokes.a: Thunder spends the whole race shouting 'Wait for me!' and nobody hears it until it arrives.

jokes.j: Two tortoises stole a snail's lunch. The police asked, 'Can you describe what happened?'
jokes.a: The snail said, 'I cannot. It all happened so fast!'

jokes.j: What is the fastest thing in a Bengaluru traffic jam?
jokes.a: The auto driver's horn. It is the only thing that gets anywhere.

jokes.j: Why is the second hand of a clock so tired by evening?
jokes.a: It runs 1,440 laps every single day and nobody has ever given it a medal.

jokes.j: What did the Earth say to the girl who said she was sitting perfectly still?
jokes.a: 'Look again. You are going round the Sun at more than one lakh kilometres per hour, and you did not even buy a ticket.'

jokes.j: How does a tortoise answer, 'Are you coming to the party?'
jokes.a: 'Yes. Tell everyone I left last Tuesday.'

jokes.j: What is the speed of one dosa on a hungry child's plate?
jokes.a: Nobody knows. The stopwatch was never fast enough.

warmup.q: A bus goes 60 kilometres in 2 hours. What is its speed?
Which two measurements do you need to find a speed?
warmup.a: A distance and the time it took.

warmup.q: What does the word 'per' mean in 'metres per second'?
warmup.a: It means 'in each'. So metres per second means metres in each second.

warmup.q: True or false: a speedometer shows the average speed of the whole trip.
warmup.a: False. It shows the speed at that moment.

warmup.q: You sit in a moving bus. Name something your speed is zero compared with.
warmup.a: The bus seat, or anything else that moves along with the bus.

warmup.q: A girl walks 2 kilometres in 30 minutes. How far does she walk in one hour at the same pace?
warmup.a: 4 kilometres. One hour is two lots of 30 minutes.

warmup.q: Which is faster, 5 metres per second or 15 kilometres per hour?
warmup.a: 5 metres per second. It is 18 kilometres per hour.

warmup.q: Light takes about 1 second to cover 3 lakh kilometres. About how long for 6 lakh kilometres?

games.title: The Hour Journey: a card game about average speed
games.players: 2 to 4 players. A parent and a child are enough.
games.context: This is a card game in which every player makes a journey that lasts exactly one hour. The player who covers the most distance has the highest average speed, and waiting time counts against everyone.

setup.art: A table with 30 journey cards and 6 delay cards cut out from a sheet and shuffled into one pile.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 36 cards from the printed sheet and shuffle them.

setup.art: Two players each holding six cards close to their chest, with a draw pile and a discard pile between them.
setup.caption: 2. Deal 6 cards to each player. Put the rest face down as the draw pile.

setup.art: A player laying three journey cards in a row on the table, with a score sheet and pencil beside them.
setup.caption: 3. After three turns each, lay down your best journey of up to 60 minutes and write its kilometres on the score sheet.

printables.title: 6 delay cards
items: Closed railway gate. Wait 10 minutes. 0 kilometres.
A cow sits in the road. Wait 10 minutes. 0 kilometres.
A flooded lane. Wait 10 minutes. 0 kilometres.
A flat tyre. Wait 10 minutes. 0 kilometres.
Waiting for the ferry. Wait 10 minutes. 0 kilometres.
A wedding procession blocks the road. Wait 10 minutes. 0 kilometres.

printables.title: Score sheet, to copy by hand: three rows for rounds 1 to 3, with columns for each player's kilometres and points
items: Round 1. Kilometres for each player, then points.
Round 2. Kilometres for each player, then points.
Round 3. Kilometres for each player, then points.
Total points for each player.

rules: Every journey lasts exactly one hour, which is 60 minutes. Any minutes you do not fill with journey cards are spent standing still and cover no distance.
A journey card shows how many minutes the leg takes and how many kilometres it covers. A delay card adds 10 minutes of waiting and 0 kilometres.
Deal 6 cards to each player. Keep your cards hidden. Put the rest face down as the draw pile.
Each player takes 3 turns, going round the table. On your turn, either draw one card and discard one card, or play a delay card from your hand in front of another player.
A delay card in front of you takes 10 minutes from your hour. A delay card you still hold at the end is thrown away.
After everyone has had 3 turns, build your journey. Lay down any of your journey cards whose minutes, plus 10 for each delay in front of you, add up to 60 or less.
Add up your kilometres. The player with the most kilometres wins the round and takes 1 point. Tied players each take 1 point.
Say it aloud: the kilometres in a one-hour journey are the journey's average speed in kilometres per hour.
If the draw pile runs out, shuffle the discard pile and carry on. Put all 36 cards back together for each new round.
Play 3 rounds. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, play one more round.

flow.do: Cut out the 36 cards from the printed sheet and shuffle them. Read the three kinds of card together: a leg of a journey, a delay and the one-hour rule.
flow.say: Every journey in this game lasts one hour. Each card is one part of the journey. Whoever goes farthest in the hour has the best average speed.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and shuffle them. Every journey lasts one hour. The farthest wins.
flow.parent: Cutting is for the grown-up if the child is under 8. Keep the cards in a bowl or an envelope after the game for next time.

flow.do: Play round 1. Deal 6 cards each, take 3 turns each, then build and add up the journeys. Say aloud which cards you chose and why.
flow.say: You have 6 cards and each one has minutes and kilometres. Which card gives you the most kilometres for its minutes? Pick your best journey of up to 60 minutes.
flow.kid: Look at your cards. Which give the most kilometres for the time? Pick your best hour.

ask.q: A 10 minute card gives 4 kilometres. A 30 minute card gives 9 kilometres. Which is the faster leg?
good: The 10 minute card. In 30 minutes it would give 12 kilometres, which is more than 9.
It covers 24 kilometres per hour and the other covers 18.

flow.think: Is the card with the most kilometres always the best one to use?

flow.do: Play rounds 2 and 3 the same way. Keep the score sheet up to date.
flow.say: Now you know the rules. Try to guess which cards are best before the others pick.
flow.kid: Play two more rounds. Write the score after each round.

ask.q: A delay card makes you stand still for 10 minutes. What does it do to your average speed?
good: It lowers it, because the time grows and the distance does not.
It takes away 10 minutes you could have used to cover distance.

flow.do: Find the speed of your best leg. Multiply the kilometres by 6 for a 10 minute card, by 3 for a 20 minute card, or by 2 for a 30 minute card.
flow.say: Pick the best leg you played. How many kilometres would it cover in a whole hour at that speed?
flow.kid: Pick your best card. Work out its kilometres for a whole hour.

ask.q: Why do you multiply by 6 for a 10 minute card?
good: Because six lots of 10 minutes make an hour.
Because the hour is six times as long.

flow.think: Which card in the pile do you think has the highest speed?

activities.title: Walk, tiptoe and hop: how far in ten claps?
activities.context: This is the idea of speed for a young child, with no numbers. You do three movements for the same number of claps and see which one goes farthest.

materials.item: chappals or soft toys to use as markers
a clear path of about 5 metres, such as a hall, a terrace or a corridor

schedule.what: Move for ten claps in three different ways, mark where you stop, then change the question and keep the distance the same.

activities.record: Draw three footprints or three arrows on a paper strip, one for each way of moving. Make the longest arrow for the one that went farthest.

setup.art: A child standing at a paper line in a corridor while a parent claps, with a chappal placed far down the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Stand at a start line. A parent claps slowly and steadily, one clap about every second.

setup.art: Three chappals on the floor at three different distances from the start line, labelled walk, tiptoe and hop.
setup.caption: 2. After ten claps, put a chappal where you stopped. Do this for walking, tiptoeing and hopping.

setup.art: A child standing at the start line with a finger pointing at the farthest chappal while the parent claps.
setup.caption: 3. Now go to the same chappal each time and count claps. Which way takes the most claps?

flow.do: Choose a start line, such as a strip of paper or a chalk mark. Practise the clapping. Clap once about every second, for ten claps, at a steady pace.
flow.say: I will clap ten times, slowly and steadily. You walk in your ordinary way until I stop clapping.
flow.kid: Stand on the line. Walk until the claps stop.
flow.parent: A steady clap is about one clap for each second. Count 'one-and, two-and' to keep time. If you are alone with the child, use a song with a steady beat.

flow.do: Ask your child to walk for ten claps and place a chappal where she or he stops. Repeat on tiptoe, and then hopping on both feet. Place a different chappal each time.
flow.say: Which one do you think will go farthest in ten claps? Why do you think so? Let us see.
flow.kid: Move for ten claps three times. Put a chappal where you stop each time.

ask.q: Which went farthest and which went the shortest?
good: Walking farthest and hopping or tiptoe the shortest, or any honest answer from the chappals.
The one with the longest gap from the line.

flow.do: Pick the chappal for the walk. Ask your child to tiptoe and then hop to that same chappal while you clap. Count the claps each time.
flow.say: The finish is the same this time. Which way takes the most claps?
flow.kid: Go to the walking chappal on tiptoe and then by hopping. Count the claps.

ask.q: Did hopping or tiptoeing take more claps to reach the same place?
good: The slower way took more claps.
The one that moved less far in each clap.

flow.do: Draw the three arrows on the paper strip together. Make the longest arrow for the movement that went farthest in ten claps.
flow.say: Draw one arrow for each way. The farthest gets the longest arrow.
flow.kid: Draw an arrow for each movement. Make the longest one for the farthest.
flow.think: If you could move for 20 claps, what would happen to the arrows?

activities.title: The fair head start: a race both people can win
activities.context: This activity needs no measuring. You and another person find a head start that makes two different walking speeds finish together, and see what the head start says about how much faster one is.

materials.item: two people who walk at their ordinary pace, such as a parent and a child, or two siblings
a straight path of 8 to 12 steps in a hall or a terrace
two chappals for markers

schedule.what: Race once, find the head start that makes a tie, then say what it tells you about the two speeds.

activities.record: Draw the path as a line. Mark the finish, the faster walker's start and the slower walker's start. Write one sentence about what the head start shows.

setup.art: A line of floor tiles between a start chappal and a finish chappal, with two people standing at the start.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a start and a finish about 10 steps apart.

setup.art: The slower walker standing several tiles ahead of the faster walker, both facing the finish.
setup.caption: 2. Give the slower walker a head start of a few tiles.

setup.art: Two people reaching the finish chappal side by side, with a third chappal showing the head start.
setup.caption: 3. Move the head start until you both arrive together.

flow.do: Mark the start with a chappal and the finish about 10 steps away with another chappal. Both of you stand at the start. Say 'go' and walk to the finish at your ordinary pace. Do not hurry.
flow.say: Walk at your usual pace and do not try to win. We want to see who naturally arrives first.
flow.kid: Both walk at your usual pace. Who arrives first?
flow.parent: If the child is the faster walker, that is fine. Either way, one will arrive first by a small amount.

flow.do: Give the person who arrived second a head start by moving them forward a few tiles. Walk again at the same ordinary paces. If one still arrives first, move the head start. Try up to four times.
flow.say: How far ahead should the slower walker start so that we arrive together? Guess, and then try it.
flow.kid: The slower walker starts ahead. Move the start until you arrive together.

good: The head start makes up for the time the faster walker saves on the rest of the path.
The slower walker covers less distance in the same time.

flow.parent: If the two of you walk at the same pace, the head start is nothing. Then one of you walks faster on purpose, like a brisk walk against a slow walk.

flow.do: When you tie, look at the path. The faster walker covered the whole path and the slower walker covered only part of it in the same time. Ask how the two distances compare.
flow.say: We both walked for the same time. Who covered more path? About how many times more?
flow.kid: Look at the two distances. Who went farther in the same time?

ask.q: If the slower walker starts half way along the path and you tie, how many times faster is the other walker?
good: Twice as fast, because she covers the whole path in the time the other covers half.
Two times as fast.

flow.do: Swap places and try walking at the speed of the other person. See if you can tie without a head start.
flow.say: Can you walk at my pace, so that the race is a tie from the same start?
flow.kid: Try to walk exactly at the other person's speed. Can you tie?
flow.think: Is it easier to keep the same speed as someone else, or to keep your own speed the same each time?

activities.title: Trip notes: the speed of your own errand
activities.context: This activity finds the average speed of a trip you were going to make anyway, such as a walk to the kirana shop or a bus ride to a relative's home, and compares it with the speed while moving.

materials.item: a phone with a map and a clock, or a watch
paper and a pencil
a grown-up to come along

schedule.what: Before leaving, note the map distance. During the trip, note start time, stops and finish time. At home, work out the two speeds.

activities.record: Write the mode of travel, the distance, the total time, the time standing still, the average speed and the speed while moving.
activities.safety: A grown-up comes along and holds the phone near roads. Cross roads only with the grown-up.

setup.art: A phone screen showing a map route from a home to a vegetable market with the distance at the top.
setup.caption: 1. Before leaving, find the distance on the map and write it down.

setup.art: A child's notebook with a list of times next to the words left home, signal, shop and back.
setup.caption: 2. Write the time at each stop along the way.

setup.art: A page with two sums, whole distance divided by whole time and the same distance divided by the time moving.
setup.caption: 3. At home, work out the average speed and the speed while moving.

flow.do: Choose a trip you would make today anyway, such as to a shop, the market, a school gate or a bus stop. Look up the distance on a phone map and write it down. If there is no map, walk 20 steps in the hall, measure that distance once with a tape, and use that for each step.
flow.say: Before we leave, how far do you think it is? What do you think our speed will be?
flow.kid: Write how far the trip is. Guess how fast you will go.
flow.parent: A child's step is about 50 centimetres, so 2,000 steps make about a kilometre. The map's walking distance is better when you have it.

flow.do: During the trip, write the time you leave, the time of each stop, such as a signal or a queue, and the time you arrive.
flow.say: Please write down the time each time we stop. We want to know how long we were standing still.
flow.kid: Write the time at the start, at every stop and at the end.
flow.parent: Keep the notebook in a pocket so the child can write at stops only.

flow.do: At home, find the whole time and the time standing still. Divide the distance by the whole time to get the average speed. Then take away the standing still time and divide the distance by the time moving.
flow.say: Which is bigger, the speed for the whole trip or the speed while moving? Why?
flow.kid: Work out two speeds. Which is bigger?

ask.q: Why is the average speed for the whole trip lower?
good: The time standing still counts in the trip but adds no distance.
The stops take time and carry no distance.

flow.think: If you took a different road or a different way of travelling, which of the two speeds would change most?

projects.title: The slowest racers: a sprout and climbing water
projects.context: In this project you measure the speed of two very slow movers, water creeping up a paper strip and a seed's shoot growing, and compare them with sums.

materials.item: a steel bowl with a cover or a plate
2 tablespoons of whole moong or chana
a clean cloth or kitchen tissue
a tall glass or steel tumbler
a strip of kitchen tissue or newspaper about 2 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres long
a pencil, a ruler with millimetres and a clock
a few drops of ink or a pinch of turmeric

schedule.what: Soak the moong or chana in water in the evening.
Drain the seeds and wrap them in a damp cloth. Then time how fast water climbs a paper strip.
Measure the shoots, rinse them and keep them warm.
Measure the shoots again at the same time of day, and rinse.
Measure the shoots a third time, and rinse.
Draw the graphs and work out the two speeds. Then compare them.

projects.record: Keep a table for the water front (minutes and centimetres) and another for the sprouts (day and the length of the longest shoot in millimetres). Draw a distance and time graph for each.

setup.art: A steel bowl of moong seeds covered by water on a kitchen counter in the evening.
setup.caption: 1. Day 1: soak the seeds overnight.

setup.art: A paper strip dipped into a tumbler of coloured water, with pencil marks drawn up the strip.
setup.caption: 2. Day 2: mark where the water front has reached each minute.

setup.art: A ruler beside a sprouting moong seed with a pale shoot, measured in millimetres.
setup.caption: 3. Days 3 to 5: measure the shoot at the same time each day.

setup.art: Two graphs on one page, a steep one for the water and a nearly flat one for the sprout.
setup.caption: 4. Day 6: draw both graphs and compare.

flow.do: In the evening, put 2 tablespoons of moong or chana in a steel bowl. Cover with water by about 2 finger-widths. Leave them for 8 to 10 hours.
flow.say: Seeds are alive. They will wake up when they drink. Where do you think they will grow from?
flow.kid: Put the seeds in water. They need to drink all night.
flow.parent: The seeds swell as they drink. In cool weather, soak for 12 hours.

flow.do: Drain the seeds and wrap them in a damp cloth inside the bowl. Put the cover on and keep the bowl in a warm, dark place. Then set up the strip. Pour 2 centimetres of water into a tumbler and stir in a few drops of ink or a pinch of turmeric. Hang one end of the strip in the water so that it touches. Draw a line at the water's edge on the strip every minute for 10 minutes, with a pencil and a clock.
flow.say: Where will the water reach after one minute? After ten? Do you think it will go up at the same speed all the time?
flow.kid: Hang the strip in the water. Every minute, draw a line where the water has got to. Do this for 10 minutes.

ask.q: Does the water climb the same distance each minute?
good: No. It climbs farther in the first minutes and slows down later.
Not steady. It slows down.

flow.parent: If the strip climbs less than 2 centimetres in 10 minutes, use a thinner strip or a fresh one. If the water climbs all the way up before 10 minutes, mark every 30 seconds and say so in the record. If the strip flops, lean it against a pencil laid across the tumbler.

flow.do: Open the cloth and look at the seeds. Measure the longest shoot with the ruler in millimetres. If there is no shoot yet, write 0. Rinse the seeds gently with water, wrap them again and keep them warm.
flow.say: Look at your seeds. Have any of them started to grow? How long is the longest bit?
flow.kid: Measure the longest shoot in millimetres. Write the number. Rinse and cover the seeds.
flow.parent: Do not worry if there is no shoot on day 3. In cool weather, put the bowl near a stove that is lit or on top of a fridge. Shoots can take another day. Write 0 and carry on.

flow.do: At the same time as yesterday, measure the longest shoot again, write the number, rinse and cover the seeds.
flow.say: How much longer is the shoot than yesterday?
flow.kid: Measure the longest shoot again. How much longer is it?

flow.do: Measure the longest shoot a third time and rinse and cover the seeds as before.
flow.say: Is the shoot growing at the same speed each day?
flow.kid: Measure the shoot one more time. Write the number.

flow.do: Draw a graph for the water with minutes across and centimetres up. Draw another for the shoot with days across and millimetres up. Work out the water's speed in millimetres per hour for the first 3 minutes. Work out the shoot's speed in millimetres per hour between day 3 and day 5 by dividing the growth by the hours.
flow.say: Which graph is steeper? How many times faster is the water than the shoot?
flow.kid: Draw both graphs. Work out both speeds. Which is bigger?

ask.q: How many times faster is the water than the shoot?
good: Many hundreds or thousands of times faster, depending on your numbers.
The water's speed divided by the shoot's speed.

flow.parent: The sprouts can be eaten in a salad or cooked. Pour the tumbler water onto a plant.
flow.think: Both are real movements. Which one is easier to notice and which one matters for the seed?

challenges.title: A timer you can trust: time a toy car without finger errors
challenges.context: This is a design problem. A finger on a phone stopwatch is slow and uneven, so you build or find a better way to time a toy car over two metres.
challenges.problem: Find a way to time a toy car over a 2-metre track so that two different people who time the same run get answers within one tenth of a second of each other. There is more than one good answer.
constraints: Use only things you can find at home. A phone is allowed, but not a special timing app made for races.
The car must be let go and never pushed, and it must run the same each time.
Time at least five runs of your method and write them down.
Compare your result with the plain stopwatch method on the same car.
materials: a toy car, a ramp made of a book and some books to raise it
a measuring tape or a ruler and paper tape
a phone with a stopwatch and a camera
a key and 25 centimetres of thread, or a steel spoon and a bottle for a dripping clock

setup.art: A toy car on a book ramp with two paper tape lines on the floor two metres apart and a phone on books filming from the side.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a 2-metre track and set the phone to film from the side.

setup.art: A child holding a phone stopwatch while a second person holds a second stopwatch at the finish line.
setup.caption: 2. Try the plain stopwatch method first and look at how much the times differ.

setup.art: A paused phone video of a toy car crossing a line with a frame counter in the corner.
setup.caption: 3. Try a better method and compare the spread of the results.

flow.do: Time the same car run five times with a plain phone stopwatch and write each time. Ask a second person to do the same on the same runs. Look at how much the times differ from run to run and from person to person.
flow.say: Is your time the same as the other person's for the same run? How big is the difference?
flow.kid: Time five runs with the stopwatch. Compare with another person's times.

ask.q: Why do the two people get different times for the same run?
good: A finger is late or early by different amounts each time.
Each person presses at a slightly different moment.

flow.do: Try the usual fixes. One person watches the start and calls 'now' while the other stops the clock, or the same person starts and stops at lines marked on the floor. Try counting a steady song beat or the swings of the key on its thread. Write five runs for each fix.
flow.say: Which fix gives the times that are closest together?
flow.kid: Try each fix five times. Write the times.

ask.q: Which method has the smallest gap between its fastest and slowest time?
good: The one whose five times lie closest together.
Whichever gives the smallest range, once you have checked.

flow.do: Try a surprising fix. Film the run from the side with the phone steady on a book, with both lines in view. Play the video one frame at a time, or in slow motion, and count the frames between the car's nose crossing the first line and the second line. Many phones record 30 or 60 frames each second, so each frame lasts 1 divided by 30 or 1 divided by 60 of a second. If your phone cannot step through a video, drop a steel spoon into a bottle every second and use the sound as a clock, or race the car against a ball rolling at a steady speed.
flow.say: A video is a quick series of pictures. How could the number of pictures give you a time?
flow.kid: Film the run. Count the pictures between the lines. Work out the time.

ask.q: Why does counting frames avoid the finger's slowness?
good: Nobody has to press a button at the right moment, so the frames are the clock.
The phone records the moment automatically and evenly.

flow.parent: Check the phone's camera settings to see its frames each second. If the video is in slow motion, say 120 frames each second, one frame is much shorter, so work with the number your phone shows.

flow.do: Compare all your methods. For each, write the fastest and slowest time of the five runs and subtract. The smaller the difference, the more trustworthy the method. Then work out the car's speed with your best method.
flow.say: Which method would you trust, and why? Does it measure the same car speed as the plain stopwatch?
flow.kid: Find which method has the smallest range. Work out the speed with it.
flow.think: Does a more trustworthy timer change what you know about the car, or only how sure you are?

general: Have a second person call 'now' at the start while another presses the stopwatch, and use the middle of five runs.
Count the swings of a key on a 25-centimetre thread. One swing takes about one second, so the count is the time.
Time over a longer distance, so that the finger's error is a smaller part of the whole time.
creative: Film the run and count frames. A video of 30 frames each second gives a clock that never gets tired or late.
Race the toy car against a ball that you roll at a steady pace, and use the ball's known time as a clock.

Put one person at each line. Each presses a stopwatch to start when the car passes the first line and the second person presses a stopwatch to stop when it passes the second line. Both fingers are late by about the same amount, so the lateness cancels.
challenges.your_turn: Build your own timer from things at home and test it on the toy car. What did you change that made the times closer together? Do you think any timer is ever exactly right?

buy.why: For the two-metre track and the trip notes. A tailor's tape or a shop's measuring tape costs about Rs 30 to 100.
buy.plan: Instead, mark a string or a strip of paper at every 10 centimetres by holding it against a 30 centimetre school ruler, and use that.

ask_kids: You walked to the shop today. About how long did it take, and about how far is it? So about how fast did you go?
When you sit in a bus, are you moving or not moving? What would you say if someone asked 'compared with what?'
Two movers cover the same distance, and one takes half the time. How many times faster is that one? How do you know?
What is the slowest thing you have watched today, and what is the fastest? How would you compare them?
A speedometer says 30, but the trip took longer than you thought. What could have happened during the trip?
If you could make one thing faster and one thing slower in your day, which would you choose? Who else would it change things for?
When you see lightning and then hear thunder, what does the gap in time tell you?
What would make a very short piece of a journey tell you more about the speed at that moment?
